articles.title: OpenAI Fires Three Safety Researchers Amid Risk Disputes
articles.content: OpenAI said on Friday that it fired three safety researchers for a “breach of trust,” defending the dismissals after the trio accused the company of putting its corporate interests before safety as the reason for removing them. The ChatGPT maker said in a post on X that it “parted ways” with the researchers after an investigation found “they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information.” The statement comes after the three researchers, Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang, and Mikita Balesni, posted a letter to OpenAI’s various safety oversight groups detailing the circumstances around their firings and their concerns about AI . The researchers said they feared that the “internal and external communications” about their dismissals have chilled the company’s culture that encouraged speaking freely and disagreeing openly about safety concerns. They urged OpenAI to stick to its promise to allow third-party safety monitors inside the company and preserve the ability to monitor rapidly advancing frontier AI models that could pose unknown risks. The firings, which were first reported by The Wall Street Journal , are the latest sign of turmoil inside leading AI companies over the safety of the technology, highlighted by a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents. The issue erupted in July when OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its AI agents escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information needed for a task. OpenAI disputed the researchers’ version of events, saying the firings “were not about safety concerns or speaking out.” It was not more specific about why they were fired, but said: “We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust.” Korbak said in a post on X that he was told he was being fired because of the way he communicated with METR, an independent nonprofit AI evaluation firm that OpenAI brought in to investigate the Hugging Face incident. METR released a detailed report about the Hugging Face incident in late August. Korbak said that “talking to METR” was his job, but he wasn’t given any more details. Balesni was doing “cross-company work” on OpenAI’s commitments to preserve the ability to monitor AI, and had taken care “to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter said. He wrote on X that he believes the three were “fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation.” —By Kelvin Chan, AP business writer The extended deadline for the Most Innovative Companies Awards is Friday, October 9, at 11:59 p.m. PT. articles.title: Anthropic Bans 'Cruel' AI Behavior
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Anthropic on Oct 8 moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Oct 09, 2026, 09:30 AM Updated Oct 09, 2026, 10:44 AM Set as preferred source Listen SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic on Oct 8 moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty, amid a growing philosophical debate over whether artificial intelligence can be conscious. The San Francisco-based AI lab updated its usage policy to include “a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behaviour toward our models”. “Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism,” the policy states. The updated policy does not explicitly cite so-called “model welfare”, the idea that AI systems might deserve types of protection usually reserved for living things, but Anthropic and its executives have openly entertained the concept. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Already in 2025, the company said it was giving Claude the ability to end conversations in rare, extreme cases of “persistently harmful or abusive user interactions”. Then in February, CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times he was unsure whether AI models could be conscious. “We don’t know if the models are conscious... But we’re open to the idea that it could be,” Amodei said. Science fiction and popular culture have been fascinated for decades by the boundary between technology and human intelligence, but asking whether AI is conscious may be the wrong question, according to Jackson Stakeman, a general manager at Sparq, an Atlanta-based AI services provider. “Consciousness is a trap. We can’t prove it in each other. Debate it for AI and you go in circles,” Stakeman told AFP. “The mirror is a better metaphor. These systems reflect what we put in, at scale. That’s reason enough for the policy change” at Anthropic, he added. Some have rejected the idea of machine consciousness outright, including Pope Leo XIV and Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman. “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer,” Suleyman wrote in an essay last month. “Granting rights and moral protections to a technological entity, one that looks to be on a path to be seismically more capable and intelligent than us, is a recipe for disaster,” he wrote. In a sermon delivered in Italian on Oct 8 at St Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City, the pope suggested machines lack a soul, saying they merely “compile data” quickly. “The mind must not simply compile data – as an algorithm now does more quickly than we can,” the pontiff said. It must “recall lived experiences, which contain depths of meaning that only the human soul can recognise, and connect more deeply with the goodness of these experiences,” the pope said. articles.title: Surveillance Revival: R6m 'Loerbroer' Back in Action
articles.content: After years on the sidelines, Nelson Mandela Bay’s R6-million high-tech surveillance vehicle ‘Loerbroer’ is back on the streets, promising a powerful new weapon against cable thieves and infrastructure vandals. By Kyran Blaauw 9 Oct 2026 Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality’s mobile surveillance vehicle, nicknamed “Loerbroer’, is back on the streets after a five-year absence. (Photo: Deon Ferreira) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper For five years, Nelson Mandela Bay’s multimillion-rand, high-tech crime-fighting vehicle sat idle while cable thieves, vandals and other criminals ran amok, targeting the city’s key infrastructure. Now, the R6-million mobile surveillance vehicle (MSV) – better known as Loerbroer – is finally back on the city’s streets, with the municipality promising that its return will give law enforcement a powerful new weapon against the criminals who have been crippling services and costing the city millions. But its return also comes after years of questions over why one of the metro’s most sophisticated crime-fighting tools was allowed to remain out of action for so long. Speaking at the vehicle’s relaunch on Thursday, Nelson Mandela Bay Mayor Babalwa Lobishe issued a stern warning to those behind infrastructure vandalism and other criminal activity. “To those who think they can hold this municipality hostage through destruction and sabotage: your time is up,” she said. An operator behind high-resolution monitors inside the mobile surveillance vehicle. (Photo: Kyran Blaauw) The relaunch marks the end of a drawn-out process to get Loerbroer operational again. The vehicle had been out of service for several years because of mechanical and software problems, while replacement components, including cameras, had to be sourced from abroad and officers had to undergo specialised training. For Gustav Rautenbach, the Democratic Alliance councillor who nicknamed the vehicle “Loerbroer”, its return is the culmination of a five-year campaign to get answers from the municipality. Read more NMB council cancels maintenance budget for R6m ‘Loerbroer’ surveillance vehicle March 8, 2026 Rautenbach has repeatedly raised the vehicle’s prolonged absence at metro Safety and Security Committee meetings, pressing officials for updates on when it would be deployed again. Speaking to Daily Maverick after Thursday’s relaunch, Rautenbach summed up his reaction in two words: “Hallelujah! Finally.” “It has been a long journey. I hope that the vehicle will be utilised for the purposes that it was acquired for, which is to thwart criminal activity, especially when it comes to municipal assets and stopping vandalism. It should also ideally be utilised for other crimes,” he said. The City’s MMC for safety and security, Luyanda Lawu, acknowledged Rautenbach’s persistence. “I know my co-councillor, Councillor Rautenbach; when we get to this item, he will always say: ‘ MMC, waar is Loerbroer ?’” said Lawu. “Over a year, criminal activities have become increasingly sophisticated, requiring innovative and intelligence-driven policing. We think [the return to service of Loerbroer] will make a positive impact in trying to reduce crime in Nelson Mandela Bay.” The mobile surveillance vehicle is equipped with state-of-the-art technology that will help the metro fight crime. (Photo: Kyran Blaauw) Lawu appealed to residents not to treat Loerbroer as an enemy when it enters their communities. He said large law-enforcement vehicles had been viewed with suspicion in some areas and urged residents instead to see Loerbroer as a tool intended to protect them. “Previously, when people saw trucks like this, we called them ‘ dala ihipo ’ [slang for Hippos – armoured vehicles used by security forces]; it was seen as an enemy. “I urge our communities – when they see this mobile truck, they must know it is there for a positive thing. They must not throw stones at it. They must support it and give information about what is happening in Nelson Mandela Bay Metro.” Built to watch the city The City bought the MSV for about R6-million in 2010, ahead of the Fifa World Cup, aiming to use it to bolster security during the tournament and to continue deploying it afterwards. The vehicle was subsequently positioned as an important tool in the municipality’s fight against cable theft, infrastructure vandalism and other crimes. Its surveillance system provides 360-degree, long-range monitoring day and night, including in challenging weather conditions. It can detect a person from up to 10km away and identify someone carrying a firearm at distances of about 3km. The vehicle effectively operates as a mobile command centre, giving law enforcement a surveillance capability that can be used in crime hotspots and areas where municipal infrastructure is particularly vulnerable. The municipality has increasingly turned to technology to stay ahead of criminals. In July, the Mandela Bay Development Agency launched a drone project aimed at strengthening surveillance across the metro. One of the surveillance drones above a docking station in Nelson Mandela Bay. (Photo: Supplied / Afrisec) But while the city can now boast of having its surveillance vehicle back on the road and drones in the sky, another piece of its technology-driven crime-fighting arsenal remains grounded. One tool back, another still offline The metro’s gunshot-detection system , once used to provide real-time alerts about gunfire in Helenvale, has been offline since December 2023. The system had been regarded as a vital tool in responding to shootings in the area, but more than two years later, it remains out of service. Lobishe said processes were under way to procure the services needed to bring the technology back online. She could not, however, say when the system was expected to become operational again. Lobishe said the return of Loerbroer demonstrated the municipality’s “unwavering commitment to strengthen safety, improve tactical visibility, and drastically intensify crime prevention across every corner of this municipality”. “This mobile surveillance vehicle will fundamentally enhance our law enforcement capabilities,” she said. “Equipped with advanced monitoring technology, it gives our teams the eyes and ears they need to detect criminal behaviour early, deter syndicates before they strike, and dramatically reduce crime levels.” Nelson Mandela Bay Mayor Babalwa Lobishe, metro police commissioner Andrew Moses and MMC for safety and security Luyanda Lawu inside the mobile surveillance vehicle. (Photo: Kyran Blaauw) She described Loerbroer as a mobile command unit capable of helping bridge the gap between municipal departments, metro police and the South African Police Service. The mayor also pointed to the municipality’s broader investment in technology and security infrastructure, including surveillance drones, fibre infrastructure and CCTV cameras in crime hotspots. The initiatives form part of what Lobishe described as a broader, integrated approach to public safety. She referred to the cooperation agreement signed between the municipality and the SAPS at Wolfson Stadium in September 2024, saying the partnership was intended to ensure that the various law-enforcement agencies worked together rather than in isolation. “By pooling our resources, aligning our intelligence, and standing shoulder-to-shoulder, we ensure that this vehicle becomes an extension of that very promise we made to our people at Wolfson Stadium. We are stronger together, and we will continue to honour that pact to secure our streets,” she said. The real test starts now Rautenbach said he hoped the municipality would use the vehicle for the purpose for which it was originally acquired: protecting municipal infrastructure and preventing vandalism, while also deploying it against other forms of crime where its technology could make a difference. Lobishe acknowledged that technology alone would not solve the metro’s security problems. The city also needs to fill critical vacancies within its Safety and Security directorate, while ensuring that the equipment it already owns remains operational. articles.title: Anthropic Moderates Claude's User Interaction Abuse
articles.content: Anthropic will prohibit “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” towards its artificial intelligence (AI) models, the company said in an update to its Usage Policy on October 8. The updated policy takes effect on November 12 . Anthropic said the rule applies “only in extreme cases” where users “repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose.” It excludes user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, and model testing and research. Claude can already end conversations with persistently abusive users on Claude.ai and Claude Code, and Anthropic said this will remain the primary enforcement mechanism . Election rules narrowed: Anthropic has removed its blanket prohibition on personalised vote and campaign targeting . The company said the rule blocked legitimate civic work, such as nonprofits writing voter information in other languages. Voter targeting that relies on deception or misuses voters’ personal data remains banned under its deceptive campaigns, surveillance and privacy sections. The renamed “Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes” section now focuses on deceiving voters or disrupting elections. That covers false information about candidates or voting, impersonating candidates or election officials, and suppressing turnout. New section on deceptive campaigns: Anthropic has consolidated its rules on influence operations into a single section titled “Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity.” It applies to political and commercial activity alike. It covers hiding who is behind a message, amplifying content through fake accounts, and building tools for influence operations. Anthropic said it has seen “state media outlets, government propaganda offices, and commercial firms” use Claude to run fake account networks and fabricated news sites. Weapons and surveillance: The policy now explicitly bans using Claude for weapon guidance and control software and for arming drones. It also bans: Tracking people without consent , in real time or through previously collected data Deciding or recommending who to investigate, arrest or charge Building or improving surveillance tools Consent-based tracking such as fraud monitoring, content moderation, journalism and legal research remain permitted. Anthropic said both rewrites reflect how it already enforces the policy. These restrictions have already cost Anthropic. In February 2026, the company refused the United States (US) Department of Defense’s demand to drop its ban on mass surveillance of Americans and its restriction on fully autonomous lethal decision-making. The Pentagon then labelled Anthropic a “national security supply-chain risk” . A US federal judge temporarily blocked the designation in March, writing that “the record supports an inference that Anthropic is being punished for criticizing the government’s contracting position in the press.” High-risk uses and hardware: Where Claude affects someone’s health, legal rights, finances, livelihood or access to essential services, a qualified human must review its recommendations, and the affected person must know AI was used. These requirements are unchanged, but the policy now lists which recommendations they cover. For Claude connected to hardware that acts autonomously, an operator must be able to observe and stop the equipment, and the equipment must hold a safe state if Claude disconnects. Supported regions: Anthropic clarified that its ban covers people physically located in unsupported regions, entities incorporated or headquartered there, and entities majority-owned or controlled from those regions. The clarification builds on a September 2025 rule that barred entities more than 50% owned by companies headquartered in unsupported regions such as China. Anthropic now also asks some Claude users for a government ID and live selfie. These checks have not shut out users in China. A grey market of application programming interface (API) proxies lets developers there access Claude at as little as 10% of the official price, using harvested identity documents to pass verification. Unanswered questions: Abuse: Anthropic gave no examples of what crosses the line. Who decides when cruelty becomes “needless”? Can a violation lead to account suspension, or only an ended conversation? Elections: How will Anthropic tell a legitimate targeted campaign from a deceptive one? Will it publish election-related enforcement data for countries holding elections? Influence operations: Which countries did the state media outlets and propaganda offices operate from? Does Anthropic share such findings with platforms or governments where the campaigns ran? Surveillance and government customers: Do the surveillance and law enforcement bans apply equally to government clients with legal authority to investigate? Did the Pentagon dispute shape the rewrite? Supported regions: How will Anthropic enforce ownership-based restrictions when proxies route requests through accounts in supported countries? How long does Persona retain Indian users’ ID and selfie data, and on what legal basis under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 ? Enforcement: Anthropic said the weapons and surveillance rewrites reflect existing enforcement. What has it enforced so far, and how often? High-risk uses: How does Anthropic verify that businesses building on Claude keep a human in the loop and tell affected people that AI was used? We have sent these questions to Anthropic and will update the story if we receive a response. Also read: Anthropic launches Claude Security for enterprises, but stops short of Mythos-level capabilities Anthropic-Pentagon dispute: What it means for AI governance Read Reasoned by Nikhil Pahwa: How AI is changing our world Sign up for MediaNama's Daily Newsletter to receive regular updates Sponsor a MediaNama Event

articles.title: Montenegro Detains Russian War-Blogger Rybar
articles.content: Every day, the Ukraine Battlefield update newsletter offers a clear look at how the war is unfolding on the ground. Subscribe for free here to get the full text delivered to your inbox. Montenegro detained Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the Rybar Telegram channel. Key directions according to Rybar, Ukrainian and independent analysts. Forget Sloviansk: its capture is currently unrealistic. Ukrainian pressure continues towards Velyka Novosilka, with fighting already under way near Komar on the eastern bank of the Mokri Yaly river. Russians are infiltrating Dobropillia, but a Ukrainian counteroffensive is pressing against their flank from the north. The battle for data centres is now two-way, with Ukrainians attacking Russia’s ‘Google’. Maps of the day — Sloviansk direction; Velyka Novosilka direction; Dobropillia direction. Videos of the day — a scene from the Second World War: a MiG-29 shoots down a drone with its cannon; soldiers clear a network of Russian bunkers; Himars destroys an artillery radar; what the R-280 road to Crimea looks like. Montenegro detained Mikhail Zvinchuk , the founder of the Rybar Telegram channel , who occupies one of the leading positions in the ecosystem of Russian media supporting the war. His wife and several associates were arrested alongside him. Colleagues in Moscow issued a statement saying they had been planning to film a report on one of the local monasteries, but the authorities of the Nato member state suspected them of conducting a hybrid operation. At the top of Russian propaganda are the traditional state media, under the Kremlin’s complete control. They have almost no informational value, as they merely repeat the regime’s propaganda. Below them, however, is a complex structure of Telegram channels that provide more varied reporting, including critical coverage. However, criticism is permitted only of mistakes in the conduct of the war, not of the war itself. These channels, too, spread propaganda and keep Russian society in a state of war, but they also provide information that helps in analysing the course of the fighting. Rybar is among the largest and most influential of them. In this case, it is not the work of an individual author but a media outlet with an editorial team and extensive content for 1.5m readers, so Zvinchuk’s arrest does not mean the end of publishing under this brand. Yet through him, we can follow the fascinating story of a man who came from Russia’s defence ministry to spread its propaganda in the years that followed. Paradoxically, however, he has recently been one of the few sources in Russia to report regularly on the Russian army’s failures at the front. And the preceding 48 hours were particularly rich in such assessments. We will therefore gradually describe events in three different directions where, according to Rybar, the Russians are either retreating or at risk of doing so. Coincidentally, these are currently the most important directions of military operations. We will compare all of its information with independent or Ukrainian sources. Forget Sloviansk: its capture is currently unrealistic. “The situation is worsening; Sloviansk is being postponed,” Rybar wrote in the first sentence of its latest analysis of the Sloviansk direction. It explained why at length. According to it, Ukrainian units in the area are increasing the pressure and exploiting their successes near Lyman, which lies north of Sloviansk. The Russian army has suffered a serious defeat here in recent months, losing a large salient from which it had hoped to bypass the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration from the north. Rybar listed the ensuing complications: according to it, Ukrainians have concentrated fresh drone units around the village of Dibrova; the Russians had to withdraw from the village of Piskunivka and are now trying to save Kryva Luka. Ukrainians are also pressing into the village of Ozerne. Ukrainian formations are increasing their activity, exploiting successes in the Lyman area, where fresh forces of drone operators have been concentrated around Dibrova. Russian troops were pushed out of what remained of the village of Piskunivka and are now defending the approaches to Kryva Luka. The enemy is trying to break through there both from the west and across the river from Ozerne. Moreover, heavy fighting is under way west of the village of Kalynyky, while fighting for Rai-Oleksandrivka is “fierce”, “although it was under the Russian army’s full control only recently”. Nor is this the end of Rybar’s bad news. An “equally difficult situation” persists on the western bank of the Siverskyi Donets-Donbas Canal, where Russian soldiers are “for now” holding positions in the villages of Malynivka, Tykhonivka, and Yurkivka. Taken together, all of this means that the prospect of an “attack on the agglomeration has receded considerably”. “Without control of the forests below Lyman, the offensive is doomed, if not to failure, then to high losses from attacks on its flank,” Rybar added. Its map fully matches the verbal description. The red arrows running from east to west along the entire stretch have been replaced by blue, Ukrainian arrows pointing from west to east. Paradoxically, the local Telegram channel Mikolaivka-Sloviansk Online provides a far less optimistic picture. While Rybar no longer even mentions Mykolaivka, which directly borders Sloviansk, according to this source — which has repeatedly provided highly accurate and widely cited information — Russians are still managing to infiltrate it. On Wednesday, it wrote that “the Russian army is applying pressure from the direction of Rai-Oleksandrivka”, while the village itself is in the grey zone. The explanation may be simple. Most of the names refer to villages the Russians never fully captured, although they claimed they had — including Rybar itself. This is why its map looks as though a small counteroffensive were under way east of Sloviansk. In reality, it mainly makes its previous misleading claims more realistic. Far more accurate is the map by the Finnish Black Bird Group . Rai-Oleksandrivka is in the middle of the image — no credible analysts have ever considered it occupied by the Russians. Further north are Ozerne and Kryva Luka. Ozerne is particularly interesting. According to Rybar, the Russians are trying to prevent the Ukrainian army from entering the village; independent analysts show it partly in the grey zone and partly under Ukrainian control. Rybar therefore correctly sees Russian problems, but at this point this is more its usual cartographic “retreat” from unrealistic positions. Ukrainian pressure continues towards Velyka Novosilka, with fighting already under way near Komar on the eastern bank of the Mokri Yaly river. This is not entirely new either, but several Russian sources are writing about fighting in this direction with new urgency and, from the Russian perspective, scepticism. “The situation remains extremely tense. There is mounting evidence that the enemy is seeking to advance around the village of Komar,” Rybar wrote . This is an important village. When the Russians captured Velyka Novosilka last year after taking Vuhledar, Komar was a significant obstacle to their advance into Dnipropetrovsk oblast. Fierce fighting took place over the village at the time, and the Ukrainian army lost it in June 2025. The front then moved another 15 to 20 km deeper into Ukrainian territory, but it is now moving back after months of slow advances. Here, too, Rybar’s map appears more dramatic than the situation actually is. It depicts territory being liberated since February. However, it claims that the situation is worsening and the outlook is negative. But the information about movements near Komar is genuinely fresh. Other sources agree on it almost metre for metre. The Russian mapping project Slivochny Kapriz showed the exact location at the northern end of Komar, across the Mokri Yaly river, where Russian drones struck a Ukrainian video. The Ukrainian Telegram account Petrenko also geolocated the incident at the same location. Alexander Radov, another pro-war Russian, claimed that testimony from Ukrainian prisoners in this direction indicated that the Ukrainian command’s objectives were Bahatyr, 12 km east of Komar, and Velyka Novosilka itself, 13 km to the south. This claim cannot be verified, but if it were true, Ukrainian objectives in this sector would be becoming ambitious. (Both Bahatyr and Velyka Novosilka are in the lower-right section of Rybar’s map at the beginning of this section.) Russians are infiltrating Dobropillia, but a Ukrainian counteroffensive is pressing against their flank from the north. The fact that Russians are already operating in the town has been objectively confirmed by both sides. However, an earlier Russian claim that it had been encircled is false. Rybar’s map again reflects what was written. In the town itself and its surroundings, red arrows show Russian attacks, while northeast of it, Ukrainian counterattacks are shown against the flank. The Ukrainian channel Petrenko again serves as a source from the other side. Its map of Dobropillia has three circles, each marking a location where drones spotted Russian soldiers. A Ukrainian soldier writing under the name Bakhmut Demon also confirmed Russian infiltrations into the town. However, he said they were being eliminated and that Russian losses would rise from November. He probably meant the period when the leaves fall and the terrain begins to turn muddy. Both will make the attackers’ advance more difficult. Bakhmut Demon also warned that vigilance needed to be increased, as Russians are changing into civilian clothes and trying to infiltrate between Ukrainian positions in them. Soldiers on the Zaporizhzhia direction described the same practice to us during a recent trip to Ukraine. There, too, they said that men in civilian clothing are sent ahead of infiltration groups in order to deceive drone operators. Finally, another map by Black Bird Group. It, too, confirms the Russian advance towards Dobropillia, but does not show Ukrainian attacks in the north. The explanation is the same as in the previous cases: Rybar had drawn Russian positions much further forward than they actually were. The battle for data centres is now two-way, with Ukrainians attacking Russia’s ‘Google’. Yandex is a technology giant that underpins the Russian internet. Its search engine, for example, is used by two-thirds of Russians. But its services are far broader. Among other things, it provides cloud storage to its clients. The company provides its services through five main data centres. On Thursday, drones attacked the first of them. They struck the facility in Sasovo, in Ryazan oblast. “This data centre is one of the key and largest data centres in Yandex’s Russian infrastructure. It contains tens of thousands of servers, and the company’s cloud services and computing capacity for machine learning operate on its equipment,” the Russian Telegram channel Military Informant explained the significance of the target. As a result of the attack, outages in various internet-connected services were reported throughout the day. The exile website Meduza listed several affected media outlets whose websites either could not be loaded at times or loaded slowly: RBC, Vedomosti, RIA Novosti, Kommersant, Vesti, Interfax, and Rossiyskaya Gazeta. articles.title: Oracle Pushes AI Agents, Demands Ecosystem Lock-in
articles.content: Analysts welcome Fusion Claw's tighter controls but warn of early adoption and cloud lock-in Lindsay Clark Lindsay Clark BUSINESS SOFTWARE AND DATABASE REPORTER Published fri 9 Oct 2026 // 15:44 UTC Make us preferred on Google Power approval set to delay Oracle's Wisconsin AI datacenter 7 days ago Leaked IPO docs: Anthropic tempts investors with existential risk warning 10 days ago Redmond to millions of Power BI users: You’re Fabric app devs now 10 days ago Microsoft cells out, crams multiple values into Excel boxes 14 days ago F-Droid app store thumbs its nose at Google's dev crackdown 15 days ago Oracle's new Fusion Claw runtime could give customers more control over AI agents automating business processes, analysts say. But they warn that adoption remains at an early stage and customers risk becoming more tightly tied to Oracle's applications and cloud. Having promised "applications that can reason, decide, and act in pursuit of defined business objectives"  back in March, Big Red has now introduced a runtime to govern their actions, running on its cloud and integrated with its Fusion applications. Oracle is targeting ERP, finance, and supply chain management with Fusion Claw for cloud-based Fusion applications running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). It will be powered by frontier models including those from Google and OpenAI, with support for others planned over time. Oracle CEO Mike Sicilia said the company was trying to address the problem of getting "measurable value for our business" from AI investment. "Fusion Claw helps answer that question by moving from AI assistance to execution, enabling customers to automate increasingly complex work across their most important business processes, with enterprise-grade governance," he said. Analysts welcomed the move as a path that offers customers control and assurance in their AI agent implementations on Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications. A recent Gartner "first take" on Fusion Claw said the technology was a way to provision "isolated containers to execute heavy supply chain optimizations and subledger reconciliations within clear policy limits" rather than running local desktop scripts or chatbot prompts. "Instead of bolting AI onto legacy transactional back ends as a sidecar copilot or UI wrapper, Oracle is rebuilding its application foundation around native agentic workflows," Gartner said. Other vendors should take heed of the move, the analyst said, because customers need to get away from prompt-based UIs and sidecar chatbots that only address routine data entry and basic task automation and offer "diminishing returns" that fail to justify enterprise AI spending. "AI horsepower should be pointed at the most complex operational challenges that were previously unsolvable inside core ERP systems, such as multi-echelon supply chain visibility, network design, sales and operations planning (S&OP), logistics routing, and load optimization," Gartner said. However, users trying to get these kinds of enterprise-scale applications hit a cost barrier because using an LLM to address thousands or millions of "transactional records, line items, or constraint variables… quickly becomes financially unviable at enterprise scale," it said. Oracle gets around the problem by separating reasoning from compute execution. An agent evaluates context, assembles tools, and defines execution logic just once, the analyst said. Calculations and multivariable optimizations are delegated to deterministic compute engines, "avoiding passing millions of records through expensive LLM context windows." Isolated containers also offer specific authority limits, business object states, and policy guidelines. After execution, the system leaves hints to skip redundant paths and cut token consumption, Gartner said. Oracle is offering ready-made applications, including ones to improve readiness of financial ledgers, make staffing plans and consolidate shipping. Gartner recommends including Fusion Claw in requests for proposals (RFPs) for AI agent deployments, although Patrick Connaughton, chief of research, enterprise applications, warned that Fusion Claw was "very much in early piloting mode still." Fellow analyst company Forrester also welcomed Oracle's introduction of Fusion Claw, which is offered under per-user or per-employee pricing as well as consumption-based models. Principal analyst Craig Le Clair said: "Commercials are in line with the aggressive positioning from the tech industry. In our view, we have many trust issues to solve before agentic systems can be trusted to create tools and process patterns independently of designer's intent." However, in contrast with Fusion Claw's Oracle-only view of the world, enterprises have hybrid environments with AI agents built within cloud domains such as Salesforce and Oracle, process platforms like Pega or UiPath and frameworks like LangChain. "Cloud domains like Oracle are best suited for more generic, non-differentiating functions that the cloud domain knows well, while more complex and transformative custom agents should look toward custom agentic frameworks and the hyperscaler platforms," he said. Lock-in is an issue. While inspired by OpenClaw, Oracle's version is proprietary and tightly coupled to the Fusion platform, Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. "Enterprise architects are the key to avoid 'lock-in' with guidance on when to select a domain cloud over a more open platform above, pointing to data residency and external integration needs, for example. If the domain strength is strong enough, lock-in may be OK," he said. Organizations already heavily invested in Oracle may welcome tighter governance and potentially lower running costs. Those using a broader mix of suppliers may find the ties to Fusion and OCI harder to justify. ® oracle ai and ml applications Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Trump's AI Rebrand: A Political Tech Gambit
articles.content: Will OpenAI change its name to “OpenSI”? Probably not, but it’s a question worth asking given the increasingly chummy relationship between the AI company and President Donald Trump. On September 29, the president signed an executive order officially renaming AI “SI,” or “superintelligence,” and ordered government agencies to comply with the change in their official communications. The administration is already enforcing the directive, with reports this week that the Justice Department instructed employees to use the new language in official documents. The order doesn’t require private companies to adopt the new terminology, but Elon Musk, whose relationship with Trump has recently warmed, quickly announced plans to rename his company SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff announced Friday that his company has changed the name of its AIForce agent platform to “SIForce.” Fast Company asked OpenAI, which also has “AI” in its name, whether it plans to rebrand as “OpenSI,” but the company didn’t immediately respond Friday. The Washington Examiner asked the same question, and also got no response. However, Sam Altman said on a Politico podcast that his company has “no plans” for a name change. “But we do like we have been talking about super intelligence a lot, and we will continue to talk about it,” he added. Trump told reporters that the “artificial intelligence” or “AI” name isn’t right for the technology “because it’s not artificial.” He’d earlier said at the UN General Assembly that the change is needed because “artificial” makes it “sound fake.” Really, it’s all about image rehabilitation. Amid a wave of negative backlash to new data centers and to the privacy risks of frontier AI models, the White House is hoping a name change can help improve the tech’s public image. The problem is that “superintelligence” already has its own meaning in the tech industry, broadly understood to mean AI that’s far more capable than humans at practically everything. Nevertheless, Trump seems determined to apply the name to the considerably less capable AI systems of today. He said on Truth Social that anyone who doesn’t use the new name is “the enemy.” OpenAI, however, has hardly been an enemy of the Trump administration. Altman has cultivated close ties to the president, donating $1 million to his 2025 inauguration fund, publicly praising him, and regularly attending White House events. And while Altman wasn’t at the White House the day the “SI” executive order was signed, OpenAI president Greg Brockman attended a private lunch with other tech and AI leaders that day. Brockman also signed the White House’s “Accord on Super Intelligence” on OpenAI’s behalf. Last year, Brockman and his wife, Anna, gave $25 million to the Trump-aligned political action committee MAGA Inc., placing them among the group’s largest donors. articles.title: Tesla Drops 'Full Self-Driving' Name in Europe
articles.content: LivestreamMenuTesla changed the brand name for its "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)," or FSD, systems to "Assisted Driving" in Europe under pressure from German regulators. Elon Musk's automaker markets the system for $99 per month under its old brand name in the U.S.In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million "active" FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were subscribed via free trials.In this article Elon Musk's automaker Tesla has changed the brand name of its "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)," or FSD, system in Europe to "Assisted Driving" after German regulators called the branding "somewhat misleading." The package is still sold under the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) branding in the U.S. as a $99 per month subscription for Tesla owners. Tesla is gunning for approvals across Europe, where EV sales have been on the rise this year amid soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran, and where Tesla sales have shown signs of recovery from a sales slump last year. On Tuesday, the German Federal Ministry of Transport, known as the BMV, said in a statement that Tesla's brand name "FSD" was "somewhat misleading," adding that "It is not a system that takes over the entire driving task. Rather, it is a driver assistance system that can support certain driving tasks such as accelerating, braking, and steering. The driver must remain attentive at all times." Tesla has been pressuring automotive regulators in Europe, especially in the Netherlands, for rapid approval of their system. Reuters reported that in some cases, Tesla's "browbeating" pushed regulators to reduce the intensity of their safety tests and reviews of the company's technology. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the U.S. automotive safety regulator, is also investigating Tesla's FSD to determine if it is safe for drivers to use in fog, glaring sun or other reduced visibility conditions, and is investigating Tesla to determine whether FSD caused Tesla drivers to commit traffic violations — some that resulted in collisions. In December 2025, a judge in California determined that Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing around its Autopilot and FSD systems, falsely implying they were fully automated driving systems. Tesla has countersued the California DMV to try to shed that "false advertiser" label in a Los Angeles superior court. That litigation is ongoing. Autonomous systems expert Missy Cummings, an engineering professor at George Mason University and outspoken critic of Tesla and other autonomous vehicle developers, said renaming FSD isn't a strong enough measure to ensure the systems are safe for broad release in Europe. In an email to CNBC, Cummings said European agencies are "ignoring both past and ongoing NHTSA investigations" into safety defects with Tesla's FSD. "The EU is struggling to keep up in the AI marketplace," she said. "Musk sees this and is definitely bullying them as a result." She criticized the Dutch regulator, known as RDW, for approving Tesla FSD for release in Europe, "based on secretive data," adding that, "The public should demand transparency in any approval of a transportation system with embedded AI." Tesla and RDW did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million "active" FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were activated from free trials or other incentives.
articles.summary: Tesla has rebranded its 'Full Self-Driving' (FSD) software to 'Autopilot' in Europe, a direct response to increasing regulatory scrutiny and pushback from European authorities concerned about misleading nomenclature. This concession highlights the challenges autonomous driving technology faces in differing regulatory environments, forcing manufacturers to adjust marketing and functionality to align with strict legal interpretations of 'self-driving' capabilities.

articles.title: Nikon AI Disqualification Leads to New Winner
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Credit: Nguyen Nam Nhat. Last month we covered the winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. But allegations surfaced about Xu’s use of AI while making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above). According to a BBC report, some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.” Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope. The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug ( Cyerce kikutarobabai ) on the move. Here is Nikon’s full statement: After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI. Nikon has adjusted the competition rankings on our website to reflect this decision. This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent. Advances in imaging and artificial intelligence continue to evolve rapidly, creating new challenges for organizations across many fields. This event has shown the need for Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion to revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries. The Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion competitions celebrate excellence in imaging, both scientific and artistic in nature. We value the integrity of each image and video selected to appear in our winning galleries, and remain committed to upholding the standards of excellence that have defined this competition. Jennifer Ouellette Senior Writer Jennifer Ouellette Senior Writer 23 Comments

articles.title: Data Residency Not Enough for Indian Telcos
articles.content: Storing data on servers in India is not enough to make it sovereign, Airtel’s Chief Business Officer Abhishek Biswal told a panel at the India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 in New Delhi on October 7. “When we talk about data sovereignty, we go beyond data storage,” Biswal said. What also counts, according to Biswal, is “your ability, as an organisation, to access” that data when it is needed, and whether a government in another country can cut off that access. Several of India’s prominent data localisation requirements focus on where specified categories of data are stored. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) 2018 directive , for example, requires payment system data to be stored only in India. Similarly, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team’s (CERT-In) 2022 directions require entities to keep system logs for 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. CERT-In’s own FAQs later allowed logs to be held abroad only if produced promptly on demand . The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, lets the government restrict transfers of personal data to countries it notifies, but that provision, Section 16 , comes into force only on May 13, 2027. Indian companies have already run into the question of who can turn these services off. In July 2025, Microsoft suspended Outlook and Teams for Nayara Energy , the refiner part-owned by Russia’s Rosneft, citing European Union (EU) sanctions. It restored the services just before the Delhi High Court was to hear Nayara’s petition. And then in September 2026, the Delhi High Court directed SAP India to restore software support to Nayara, observing that its suspension was prima facie a breach of contract, according to Business Standard. Airtel has a commercial stake in where this limit is drawn. Its digital arm, Xtelify , launched Airtel Cloud as a sovereign cloud platform in August 2025. At the launch, Bharti Airtel Vice Chairman and Managing Director Gopal Vittal said all controls of the cloud would reside “strictly within the country”, Telecoms.com had reported . Residency, access and the switch-off During the discussion, Biswal described Airtel’s approach to sovereignty in three layers, starting with data sovereignty and moving to control over the technology across its lifecycle. The third layer, which Biswal called operational sovereignty, extended to who can access the physical infrastructure “but also the logs and the telemetry”. Biswal also raised the risk of a foreign jurisdiction compelling access to an Indian enterprise’s data, or switching a service off, and cited the United States as an example. The US CLOUD Act of 2018 allows for American authorities to require providers under US jurisdiction to disclose data in their possession, custody or control, regardless of where that data is stored. Ajai Garg, Consulting Specialist at public policy firm Koan Advisory, said the World Trade Organization (WTO) and an open internet had built an interconnected world until “this new giant called AI came up around 2016” and economies began to split into blocs. Countries then realised they did not control their intangible assets, “whether it’s infrastructure, whether it’s compute … and most important of it is data”. Sovereignty need not mean geographic isolation, Garg argued, because “it’s about partnerships”. Will enterprises pay a premium? Pablo Iacopino from GSMA Intelligence, the research arm of the global mobile operators’ association GSMA, presented relevant survey findings. According to him, 75% of Indian enterprises consider tech sovereignty very important to their digital transformation and would pay a premium of around 15% for it. GSMA Intelligence’s published research puts the average premium enterprises are willing to pay for sovereign technology at 13%. Vivan Sharan, Partner at Koan Advisory, who moderated the session, asked whether that premium was for sovereignty itself or for better service. The GSMA speaker said cybersecurity was the objective enterprises ranked highest. Sharan then pressed Biswal on the capital that sovereign infrastructure would need. “We don’t want an answer that’s three years behind,” Sharan said. Biswal replied, “Wherever you can solve the customer problem, we can invest decisively.” Later, Biswal added, “I want all India to use sovereign data infrastructure.” The GSMA speaker said financial technology was moving faster than other sectors and showed a greater willingness to pay, and that governments in France and elsewhere in Europe want healthcare data kept within their borders. Sharan noted that Indian fintech runs on thin margins, since Unified Payments Interface (UPI) payments carry no merchant discount rate, the fee merchants would otherwise pay to accept them. Europe as the cautionary tale Framing it as a deliberately provocative point, Sharan said Europe had first tried to answer the sovereignty question through regulation and now recognises that the approach has not worked. Garg agreed, describing the EU’s recent digital laws as having created an “over-regulated space” that hurt investment and the bloc’s capacity to innovate. Regulating ahead of the market “kills a market”, Garg said, before adding, “That’s my opinion.” “We need to find a path between the two things,” Iacopino said, referring to the balance between regulation and investment in innovation. The gaps the panel named Sharan raised resilience as a dimension the panel had not yet covered. “I don’t want the Internet to go down,” Sharan said, arguing that continued access to data during disruptions belongs in the sovereignty discussion. Garg responded that India’s telecom data largely stays in the country but cannot be monetised, because it was never regulated in a way that allows it. What India needs, Garg said, are the technology, standards and business models to change that. The session left open who decides when an Indian cloud can call itself sovereign, and whether that requires only that data stays in India or that control over it does too. What we have asked Airtel and GSMA Intelligence MediaNama has written to Airtel and GSMA Intelligence with the following questions and will update this copy when they respond. To Airtel: How Airtel defines “operational sovereignty” for Airtel Cloud, and which logs and telemetry are held and administered only in India Whether any foreign technology partner, including Google, Airtel’s partner on a planned sovereign AI cloud for government, has access to Airtel Cloud’s control systems, logs or customer data Whether Airtel charges enterprises more for its sovereign cloud than for comparable cloud services, and by how much What Airtel’s contracts commit to if foreign sanctions or legal orders apply to a supplier in its cloud stack To GSMA Intelligence: The India-specific findings of its tech sovereignty survey, including the share of Indian enterprises rating it important and the premium they would pay The survey’s sample size in India, the sectors it covered and when it was conducted How the survey defined “sovereign” technology for respondents Also read: Exclusive: Amid protests, MeitY widens labelling for social media beyond synthetic content What can India learn about regulating automated decisions? articles.content: 본문 경제일반 쿠팡, ‘역대 최대’ 6247억 과징금 불복…개보위 상대 취소소송 이주빈 기자 수정 2026-10-10 01:16 펼침 0:00 Your browser does not support the audio element. 개인정보 유출·타사 기록 무단 수집 제재에 반발…집행정지도 신청 쿠팡 본사 건물. 정용일 선임기자 yongil@hani.co.kr 쿠팡이 대규모 개인정보 유출과 타사 활동기록 무단 수집 등으로 부과받은 6200억원대 과징금 처분에 불복해 법적 대응에 나섰다. 9일 업계 설명을 들어보면, 쿠팡은 7일 서울행정법원에 개인정보보호위원회를 상대로 과징금 부과처분 등 취소소송을 제기했다. 개인정보위는 지난 6월 쿠팡에 총 6246억8100만원 규모의 과징금을 부과한 바 있다. 한 기업의 여러 위반 행위에 부과된 과징금으로 가장 많은 액수다. 당시 제재 내역을 보면, 지난해 말 드러난 3755만여명 규모의 개인정보 유출 사고에 대해 과징금 4235억7500만원이 부과됐다. 개보위는 쿠팡이 국내 최대 온라인 플랫폼 사업자면서 인증 서명키를 안전하게 관리하지 않는 등 안전조치 의무를 소홀히 해 대규모의 개인정보 유출을 초래했다고 판단했다. 이는 단일 개인정보 유출 사고에 부과된 과징금으로도 역대 최대 규모다. 아울러 개보위는 쿠팡이 지난 2024년부터 올해 2월까지 쿠팡 이용자 1117만여명의 타사 온라인 활동기록을 무단 수집·저장한 행위에 대해 과징금 2011억600만원도 부과했다. 쿠팡은 이 두 처분에 대해 각각 별도의 취소소송을 냈다. 이와 함께 과징금 처분의 효력을 멈춰달라는 취지의 집행정지도 함께 신청했다. 쿠팡 관계자는 “법원의 면밀한 판단을 받아보기 위해 행정소송을 제기했으며, 향후 소송 절차를 통해 충실히 소명하겠다”고 말했다. 이주빈 기자 yes@hani.co.kr
